title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Central pathway. Bilateral: redundancy and sound localisation.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Ear canal. Tube resonance amplifies 2.5-3 kHz, the range of speech consonants.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Cochlea. 2.5 turns; scala vestibuli and tympani (perilymph), scala media (endolymph); stiff narrow base = high frequencies, wide floppy apex = low.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Middle ear. Eardrum and ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) match air to fluid impedance, raising pressure ~22×; without it ~99% of energy would be reflected.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Inner hair cells. True sensory receptors converting vibration into nerve signals.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Outer hair cells. Biological amplifier sharpening basilar membrane vibration.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Pinna. Captures sound and filters it by direction (head-related transfer function) to help localisation.
Mechanical wave; frequency (pitch), amplitude (loudness), phase; c ≈ 343 m/s in air; λ = c/f.
dB SPL = 20 log₁₀(P/20 µPa); +10 dB = 10× intensity ≈ perceived doubling; range 20 µPa-20 Pa.
Loudness is subjective; perception grows logarithmically; ear most sensitive 2-4 kHz, so equal SPL ≠ equal loudness.
Pinna: collection, directional filtering (HRTF). Canal: resonance 2.5-3 kHz. Eardrum: acoustic → mechanical.
Impedance matching air → fluid via ossicle lever; pressure ×22; prevents ~99% reflection.
Scala vestibuli and tympani (perilymph), scala media (endolymph, organ of Corti); base stiff/narrow = high, apex wide/floppy = low.
Inner: transduction (true receptors). Outer: amplification and tuning.
Auditory nerve → cochlear nucleus → superior olive → inferior colliculus → medial geniculate body → auditory cortex; bilateral.
Conductive: air ↓, bone normal (wax, otitis media, otosclerosis). Sensorineural: both ↓ (noise, presbycusis, ototoxic drugs). Mixed: both.
Aid: amplifies poorly heard frequencies (mild-moderate sensorineural). Implant: stimulates the auditory nerve when hair cells are destroyed.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Compton effect. Photon transfers part of its energy to a loosely bound outer electron and is scattered with lower energy.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Heavy charged particles. Interact mainly with electrons; energy loss (LET) rises as they slow, peaking at the end of range (Bragg peak).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Electrons. Ionise or excite atomic electrons along a broken path; deflected by nuclei they emit braking X-rays (Bremsstrahlung), used in X-ray tubes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Photoelectric effect. Photon fully absorbed by a bound (mostly K) electron, which leaves; vacancy filling gives fluorescence X-rays or Auger electrons.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Photons. No mass or charge; interact randomly; attenuation grows with density and Z and falls with energy.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Materialisation. High-energy photon near a nucleus creates an electron-positron pair.
Direct: charged particles (β⁻, β⁺, α, protons). Indirect: photons (X, γ) and neutrons.
LET: energy lost per unit length (∝ q²nZ/v²). LID: ion pairs per unit length. LET = W × LID.
Energy loss rises as the particle slows, peaking at the end (Bragg peak); protontherapy targets tumours; α dangerous internally.
With electrons: ionisation or excitation. With nuclei: Bremsstrahlung (X-ray tubes, accelerators).
N = N₀e^(−µx); µ depends on Z, density, energy; half-value layer X½ = ln2/µ.
Photoelectric (absorbed by bound K electron), Compton (outer electron + scattered photon), materialisation (e⁻e⁺ pair > 1.022 MeV).
Efficiency (intrinsic, extrinsic), background, energy resolution, dead time.
Scintillation (NaI + PM: gamma camera, PET), gas (ionisation chamber, proportional counter, Geiger-Müller), dosimeters (film, TLD, OSL, electronic).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Accommodation. Ciliary muscle contraction relaxes the zonule so the lens bulges and power increases for near vision.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Anterior corneal surface. (1.377 − 1)/0.0078 ≈ +48 D: the strongest surface, because of the air-cornea index jump.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Posterior corneal surface. (1.337 − 1.377)/0.0065 ≈ −6 D, slightly diverging.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Anterior lens surface. (1.42 − 1.337)/0.010 ≈ +8 D.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Posterior lens surface. (1.337 − 1.42)/(−0.006) ≈ +14 D.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Total power. ≈ 64 D at rest: an emmetropic eye focuses objects at infinity on the retina.
Fermat's principle; rays travel straight in homogeneous media; Snell-Descartes reflection and refraction (n₁ sin i₁ = n₂ sin i₂); n = c/v.
P = (n₂ − n₁)/r in dioptres (r in metres); positive converging, negative diverging.
Anterior cornea +48 D, posterior cornea −6 D, anterior lens +8 D, posterior lens +14 D; total ≈ 64 D.
Ciliary muscle contracts → zonular fibres relax → lens becomes more convex → power increases for near vision.
Remotum: far point without accommodation (infinity if emmetropic). Proximum: near point at maximal accommodation (~10 cm child, ≤ 25 cm adult).
Age-related lens hardening, accommodation < 4 D, near point > 25 cm; converging lenses; later in myopes.
Diplopia: images on non-corresponding retinal points. Amblyopia: suppression of one eye; patch the healthy eye before age 6; irreversible after ~10.
VA = 1/α; normal: 1′ = 10/10; 5′ = 2/10; measured with optotypes.
Myopia: image in front, diverging lens. Hyperopia: behind, converging lens. Astigmatism: non-spherical cornea, cylindrical lens.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: α decay. Heavy nuclei (N > 126) emit a helium nucleus (2 p + 2 n).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: β⁻ decay. Neutron → proton; emits an electron and an antineutrino sharing the energy; used in targeted radionuclide therapy.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: β⁺ decay. Proton → neutron; the positron annihilates with an electron into two 511 keV photons at 180°: the basis of PET.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Electron capture. A proton captures a K-shell electron (Z → Z − 1); the vacancy is filled with emission of fluorescence X-rays or Auger electrons; favoured in heavy nuclei with < 1.022 MeV.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: γ emission. An excited nucleus left after decay releases photons; isomeric if delayed (e.g. ⁹⁹ᵐTc).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Decay law. Activity A(t) = A₀·e^(−λt); after n half-lives A = A₀/2ⁿ; after 10 half-lives ≈ A₀/1024.
Isotopes: same Z. Isobars: same A. Isotones: same N. Isomers: same nucleus, different energy states (⁹⁹ᵐTc).
1 eV = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ J; 1 u ≈ 931 MeV/c²; electron 0.511 MeV.
Ionisation: electron ejected, ion formed. Excitation: electron moved to an outer shell.
Excess neutrons; n → p + e⁻ + antineutrino; energy shared; used in radionuclide therapy.
Excess protons, > 1.022 MeV; positron annihilates with an electron → two 511 keV photons at 180°.
Excess protons, low energy, heavy nuclei; K electron captured (Z − 1); X-ray fluorescence or Auger electrons.
α: heavy nuclei (N > 126) emit ⁴He. γ: de-excitation photons, Z unchanged; isomeric if delayed.
N = N₀e^(−λt), A = A₀e^(−λt); Bq = 1 decay/s; 1 Ci = 3.7×10¹⁰ Bq; T = 0.693/λ; after n T: A₀/2ⁿ.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Physical stage. Energy deposited in femtoseconds by ionisation and excitation.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Chemical stage. Radiolysis of water (65% of the body) forms •OH (oxidant) and •H radicals; oxygen amplifies damage.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Molecular lesions. Direct bond breakage or indirect radical attack on DNA, proteins, membranes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Cellular stage. Immediate death (very high doses), apoptosis, mitotic death, or survival with mutations.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Late effects. Cancerisation years later: probability rises with dose, no threshold.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hereditary effects. Mutations transmitted to offspring if germ cells are hit.
Radiation (type, energy, trajectory), organism (cells, tissues, species), irradiation conditions (dose, dose rate).
Absorbed D (Gy = J/kg). Equivalent H_T = D × W_R (Sv). Effective E = Σ H_T × W_T (Sv).
Photons and electrons 1; protons 5; neutrons 5-20 by energy; α 20.
10⁻¹⁵ s ionisation, 10⁻⁵ s free radicals, seconds-minutes molecular lesions, days-weeks cell death, years cancer, descendants mutations.
Radiation splits water into •OH (oxidant) and •H; oxygen forms more toxic radicals, increasing radiosensitivity.
Double-strand breaks (most lethal), single-strand breaks (repairable), base and sugar damage, cross-links.
Immediate necrosis (very high doses), apoptosis (lymphocytes, oocytes), mitotic death, indirect death.
Radiation type, oxygen, temperature, repair capacity, proliferation rate (marrow, gonads, mucosa high), cell cycle (M high, S low).
Deterministic: threshold, severity rises with dose (cell death). Stochastic: probability rises with dose, no threshold (cancer, hereditary).
0.3-1 Gy lymphopenia; 1-2 Gy nausea; 2-4 Gy marrow syndrome; 4-6 Gy aplasia, LD50 ≈ 4-4.5 Gy; > 6 Gy gastrointestinal.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Contamination. Deposit on skin or clothes; intake by inhalation, ingestion or wounds (I-131 to thyroid, Sr-90 to bone).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: External exposure. Source outside the body: reduce time, increase distance, use shielding (lead aprons, screens, syringe shields).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Justification. Every exposure must bring a net benefit; a useful exam changes patient management; the prescriber is responsible.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Limitation. Workers A: 20 mSv/year whole body; public: 1 mSv/year; pregnancy: < 1 mSv to the abdomen.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Optimisation. As Low As Reasonably Achievable, considering technical, social and economic factors.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biophys1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Zoning. Controlled area: dose could exceed 3/10 of a limit; supervised area: over 1/10; marked and access-restricted.
Technical, legal and administrative measures protecting humans and the environment from ionising radiation while allowing its justified, controlled use (risk-benefit).
International: ICRP (1928), UNSCEAR, IAEA. Europe: Euratom. Morocco: CNRP, AMSSNuR.
Cosmic (0.2 mSv/yr at sea level, higher at altitude), soil radionuclides U-238, Th-232 (0.3-0.5), internal K-40 (0.25).
Artificial ~0.1 mSv/yr (industry, fallout); medical ~1 mSv/yr (diagnosis, therapy).
External exposure (source outside), external contamination (deposit on skin/surfaces), internal contamination (inhalation, ingestion, wounds).
Justification (net benefit), optimisation (ALARA), limitation (dose limits).
Category A 20 mSv/yr (skin 500, lens 150); category B 6 mSv/yr (skin 150, lens 45); public 1 mSv/yr; pregnancy < 1 mSv abdomen.
Controlled (> 3/10 of limit) and supervised (> 1/10) areas; source, environment and worker controls; passive TLD/OSL, ring and electronic dosimeters.
